disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating accompanied by a sense of loss of control, followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives/diuretics, fasting, or excessive exercise to prevent weight gain. Individuals typically have an overvaluation of body shape and weight, but unlike anorexia nervosa, body weight is usually in the normal or overweight range, which can delay recognition by others. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress, interpersonal difficulties, and changes in routine or role demands. Clinically, it must be distinguished from binge-eating disorder (which lacks regular compensatory behaviors) and from normal dieting or occasional overeating by its frequency, loss of control, and impact on psychosocial functioning and health.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Adam’s amusement park announced an expansion and he began informally taking on extra responsibilities to position himself for a shift‑lead promotion. His hours became irregular with late‑night events, missed breaks, and frequent access to leftover concession food, while he simultaneously pushed himself to "look the part" of a young, energetic leader among mostly younger co‑workers. Over time, he fell into a cycle of using food during long, stressful shifts or after late‑night jam sessions, then trying to undo it with increasingly extreme routines on his hiking days and at the community center gym. He sought psychiatric care after a co‑worker commented on how exhausted he looked during a staff basketball game and he realized how much time and mental energy he was losing to planning around these eating and exercise patterns instead of his hoped‑for promotion or event‑planning goals.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like I’m constantly trying to make up for what I eat with these intense workouts and routines, and it’s taking over my life.

narrative.stressor: Around 17 months ago, Linda’s youngest child moved out and her husband shifted to partial retirement, leaving her household routines and sense of daily purpose markedly changed. With more unstructured time and a quieter home, she began oscillating between busy spurts of quilting, gardening, and sorority work and stretches of late‑evening TV and road‑trip snacking, all while becoming more self‑conscious about age‑related body changes and her image as a health professional in her community. What started as casual comfort eating during lonely evenings gradually turned into secretive episodes around food, followed by drastic attempts to "get back on track" before church gatherings or sorority events. She finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after her primary‑care doctor noticed a pattern of weight fluctuation and lab abnormalities during an annual visit and gently questioned how much control she felt she had over her eating.
narrative.chief_complaint: When I start eating, especially in the evenings, I feel like I lose control and can’t seem to stop myself.

narrative.stressor: About a year and five months ago, Thomas was advised by his cardiologist to watch his diet and lose some weight after a minor cardiac scare, which he took as a personal challenge in the context of his competitive nature and belief in self‑reliance. He began tracking his meals meticulously, but the combination of dietary restrictions, long stretches of solitary hobby time, and anxiety about his health led to episodes where he would eat far more than planned in the evenings, then attempt to undo it through increasingly aggressive methods he kept to himself. His garden club friends noticed he seemed preoccupied with what he had eaten and joked nervously about his "old man crash diets," prompting him to feel ashamed and more secretive. He ultimately presented for psychiatric evaluation after his daughter, who was visiting from out of state, saw how distressed he became after a family meal and urged him to talk to someone about how he was managing his eating and health fears.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ll sit down to eat and end up putting away way more food than anyone else, more than I ever planned, and it scares me.
